summary: Discusses how often RTCP feedback for congestion control can be sent, and whether RTCP is suitable for congestion control of unicast interactive multimedia. It is an informational discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: A video call needs to hear back quickly whether the road is jammed. This looks at how often those reports can be sent.

questions: how often can rtcp feedback be sent
how often can rtcp send feedback
subtitle: How often video calls can report network jams without wasting bandwidth.

tldr.problem: Video calls need frequent feedback about network congestion, but RTCP feedback packets are large and consume precious bandwidth. How can this feedback be sent efficiently without slowing down the connection?
tldr.mechanism: Instead of reporting on every single packet, RTCP can send detailed feedback once per few video frames, balancing responsiveness against overhead. Reduced-size RTCP packets and IPv6 considerations help minimize the bandwidth cost.
tldr.outcome: RTCP can work for congestion control if designed to accept feedback every few frames rather than per-packet. This is slower than TCP but practical for video at reasonable bandwidth levels.

today: RFC 9392 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. It remains the authoritative analysis of RTCP feedback timing constraints for congestion control in interactive multimedia.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
WebRTC video calls require congestion control to adapt when the network is congested, preventing the session from overwhelming the connection. To work, the sender must receive frequent feedback from the receiver about network conditions, packet loss, and delays. The question is: how often can this feedback be sent using RTCP without the feedback itself consuming so much bandwidth that it defeats its purpose?

This RFC analyzes the overhead of RTCP congestion control feedback in two realistic scenarios: voice telephony and point-to-point video conferences. It shows that the answer depends on the session's bandwidth, codec frame rate, and whether reduced-size RTCP packets are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Video calls need to know when the network is jammed so they can send less video. Someone has to send that news back. This memo figures out how often that news can be sent without taking up too much of the network itself.

sections.title: Considerations for RTCP Feedback
sections.content:
Several key trade-offs shape RTCP feedback design. TCP sends acknowledgements at least every 0.5 seconds, but this works partly because acknowledgements can ride on return data packets. For RTP media, feedback often travels separately, so frequent reports become expensive.

A practical congestion control algorithm might send feedback once per video frame, every few frames, or once per network round-trip time. The algorithm's rate of adaptation matters: if the video codec only adjusts bitrate every 100 milliseconds, sending feedback every 10 milliseconds adds no value.

The main tension is between responsiveness and overhead. Reduced feedback frequency slows the control loop but saves bandwidth. RTP standards have long accepted a 5% overhead for RTCP, but for congestion control at lower bitrates, this can dominate.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP says to send news back every half second, but video can send news less often. The slower the video adapts, the less often it needs to hear about jams.

sections.title: Voice Telephony Example
sections.content:
A two-party VoIP call using the Opus codec (typical 20 ms frames) shows the math. If feedback is sent every two frames (40 ms), using only compound RTCP packets with IPv4, the overhead is about 57 kbps. Sending feedback every 16 frames (320 ms, once per second) drops it to 2.8 kbps.

Using reduced-size RTCP packets (RFC 5506), where some reports omit the sender report and source description, cuts this in half: 2.2 kbps for the once-per-second case. IPv6 adds roughly 20 octets per packet, increasing overhead by about 15% on narrow links.

The key insight is that voice can tolerate infrequent feedback without sacrificing control quality, because the codec adapts slowly.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone call with tiny packets every 20 milliseconds can send feedback every second without breaking things. That keeps the feedback bandwidth to a couple of kilobits per second.

sections.title: Point-to-Point Video Conference
sections.content:
A video call at 1024 kbps with 30 frames per second, sending feedback for each frame, covers 3 video packets and 2 audio packets per report. The RTCP overhead is about 127.5 kbps, or 12% of the data rate. This is acceptable but significant.

At 4096 kbps, the same structure yields only 2% overhead. Lower bitrates (100 kbps) can reach 34% overhead, making per-frame reporting impractical. Reduced-size reports and less frequent reporting help: alternating compound and reduced-size RTCP cuts the 1024 kbps case to about 92 kbps, or 9% overhead.

IPv6 increases overhead slightly, but the effect diminishes at higher bitrates, where header costs matter less.
sections.plainLanguage: A video call at 1 megabit per second can send detailed feedback once per frame if it uses smaller packets sometimes. A very low-bandwidth call might only send feedback every few frames.

sections.title: Practical Implications
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that RTCP, as currently designed, cannot send per-packet congestion feedback at reasonable overhead. However, it works well when configured to send feedback every few frames or every network round-trip time.

The detailed feedback RTCP provides (loss bitmaps, relative arrival times, ECN marks per packet) enables effective congestion control even if sent infrequently. The format described in RFC 8888 is sufficient; optimizations come mainly from using reduced-size packets and spreading feedback less densely.

For WebRTC systems, this means the congestion control algorithm must be designed to work with the frequency of feedback RTCP naturally provides, not assume per-packet awareness.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP works if you send it every few frames, not every packet. The sender gets enough information to slow down when needed, even if it hears about jams a little late.
